### Final natural-language hypothesis (saved verbatim to `artifacts/HYPOTHESIS.txt`)

> HYPOTHESIS (NLSY79 1989 cross-section, n=12,686, ages 24-32): In the full sample, AGE has a strong negative linear association with the probability of reporting dissaving (DISSAVED=1): a logistic regression of DISSAVED on AGE adjusted for GENDER, log(1+INCOME), BMI, BLACK, and HISPANIC with HC1 robust SE gives an AGE coefficient of −0.0467 (SE 0.0092, p≈3.5e-7), an odds ratio of 0.954 per +1 year of age (95% CI 0.937–0.972), and an average marginal effect of −0.84 percentage points per +1 year of age (bootstrap 95% CI −1.12 to −0.56 pp). A likelihood-ratio test of an added quadratic AGE term is marginally significant (chi-square = 4.01, df = 1, p = 0.0453), suggesting mild concavity, but the linear specification remains the parsimonious description over this narrow 9-year age window. **CRITICAL CAVEAT — the apparent age gradient is largely an artefact of mean imputation**: when restricted to the 8,430 respondents whose INCOME/BMI are not mean-pinned, the AGE coefficient for DISSAVED collapses to +0.0001 (SE 0.0107, p = 0.991, OR ≈ 1.00); the corresponding multinomial AMEs on the non-imputed sub-sample shrink to 0.10 / −0.05 / −0.04 pp for save-more / same / save-less. Mean-pinned rows (~33% of the data, mean age 28.3 vs 27.6) almost never have DISSAVED = 1 (rate 1–11% vs 29% in non-imputed). Among respondents with substantive data there is no detectable linear association between AGE and DISSAVED. Other caveats: empirical age range is only 24–32 (a 9-year window, not a life-cycle description); no survey weights provided; marital status, employment, education and parity — strongly predictive of household savings behaviour at these ages — are not in the supplied file; INCOME has no documented scale and is therefore not interpreted in dollars; cohort is a single 1989 cross-section so the analysis is associational, not causal.

### (a) Primary model coefficients (M1 linear AGE; M2 quadratic; LPM robustness)

**Logit of DISSAVED on AGE + controls (HC1 robust SE, n=12,686)**

| Variable | Coef | SE (HC1) | z | p | OR | OR 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| const | −0.3582 | 0.2713 | −1.32 | 0.187 | 0.70 | 0.41 – 1.19 |
| **AGE** | **−0.0467** | **0.0092** | **−5.09** | **<0.001** | **0.954** | **0.937 – 0.972** |
| MALE | −0.2014 | 0.0421 | −4.78 | <0.001 | 0.818 | 0.753 – 0.888 |
| log(1+INCOME) | 0.1190 | 0.0236 | 5.04 | <0.001 | 1.126 | 1.075 – 1.180 |
| BMI | 0.0041 | 0.0036 | 1.15 | 0.251 | 1.004 | 0.997 – 1.011 |
| BLACK | 0.2077 | 0.0501 | 4.15 | <0.001 | 1.231 | 1.116 – 1.358 |
| HISPANIC | 0.1014 | 0.0597 | 1.70 | 0.089 | 1.107 | 0.984 – 1.244 |

- Average marginal effect of AGE on probability scale: **−0.835 pp / +1 year** (bootstrap 95% CI −1.121 to −0.562).
- Model fit: logLik = −6884.63, McFadden pseudo-R² = 0.0058, AIC = 13,783.27.

**M2: same as M1 plus AGE² (LR test for quadratic age)**

| Variable | Coef | SE | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| AGE | +0.4354 | 0.2432 | 0.073 |
| AGE² | −0.00869 | 0.00438 | 0.047 |

- LR test M1 vs M2: **chi² = 4.010, df = 1, p = 0.0453** → quadratic term is *marginally* significant at α=0.05 (linear specification remains parsimonious; the concavity implies the marginal decline in Pr(DISSAVED) is steepest at the youngest ages and tapers toward age 32).
- LPM Wald test on AGE² from a comparable OLS: chi² = 3.56, p = 0.059 (same conclusion).

**LPM with HC1 SE (robustness)**

| Variable | Coef | SE (HC1) | t | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AGE | −0.00839 | 0.00164 | −5.11 | 3.1e−7 |

Interpretation: each +1 year of age reduces Pr(DISSAVED = 1) by **0.84 pp** on the linear-probability scale (consistent with the logit AME).

### (b) AGE partial-dependence / marginal-effect plot

`artifacts/age_partial_dependence.png` (and matching `.svg`) shows Pr(DISSAVED=1) implied by both specifications at each AGE value in {24,...,32}, holding other covariates at their empirical distribution (partial-dependence on AGE) with 95% bootstrap CI (B = 200). Empirical DISSAVED rates per AGE are overlaid.

Predicted PDP (full sample, M1 linear): Pr(DISSAVED=1) declines monotonically and approximately linearly from 0.269 at age 24 to 0.202 at age 32 (range = 0.067, ≈ 0.83 pp / +1 year). The M2 quadratic overlay tracks M1 closely but is slightly flatter at the youngest ages and steeper toward 32, with wider CI.

Underlying numerical data is dumped to `artifacts/age_partial_dependence.data.json`.

### (c) Sensitivity — non-mean-imputed sub-sample (N = 8,430)

| Spec | M1 coef(AGE) | SE | p | OR | AME pp/yr | M2 LR χ² | LR p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full N=12,686 | −0.0467 | 0.0092 | 3.5e−7 | 0.954 | −0.835 | 4.010 | 0.0453 |
| **Non-imputed N=8,430** | **+0.0001** | **0.0107** | **0.991** | **1.000** | **+0.002** | **0.336** | **0.562** |

The headline negative age effect **essentially disappears** once the 4,256 rows whose INCOME (31%) or BMI (20%) is pinned at the column mean are excluded. Those flagged rows are slightly older (mean age 28.3 vs 27.6) and have DISSAVED rates of only 1–11% vs 29% in non-imputed rows, creating a spurious negative association between AGE and DISSAVED in the full sample.

LPM robustness on the non-imputed sub-sample: AGE coef = −0.0001, SE = 0.0022, p = 0.99.

### (d) Auxiliary multinomial logit across {save-more / same / save-less}

**Full sample** (HC1 SE, n = 12,686, reference = save-more, base rates 0.39 / 0.38 / 0.24):

- Coefficients for AGE: −0.110 (z = −11.3) in the "same" equation; −0.100 (z = −9.6) in the "save less" equation.
- Average marginal effects per +1 year of AGE:

| Category | AME (pp / year) |
|---|---|
| save-more | **+2.47** |
| same / no-savings | **−1.59** |
| save-less (=DISSAVED) | **−0.88** |
| sum | 0.00 (check ✓) |

- PDP across ages from the model: at AGE=24 → save-more 30%, same 43%, save-less 27%; at AGE=32 → save-more 48%, same 32%, save-less 20%. The model captures ~80–85% of the empirical compositional shift (empirical at 24: 31/43/26; at 32: 55/27/18); most of the age-driven movement is out of "no-savings" into "save-more", with a smaller reduction in dissaving.

**Non-imputed sub-sample** AMEs for AGE: save-more +0.10 pp, same −0.05 pp, save-less −0.04 pp — effectively zero, mirroring the logit sensitivity finding.

Plot: `artifacts/multinomial_age_decomposition.png` (and `.svg`).

### (e) Workflow description (for `payload.workflow`)

- **Data:** 12,686 × 9 NLSY79 1989 cross-section (`data/nls_bmi_processed.csv`), no missingness on the supplied variables.
- **Outcome:** DISSAVED ∈ {0,1}, marginal binary per researcher's directive; auxiliary multinomial logit on {save-more, same, save-less} ternary outcome.
- **Exposure:** AGE (integer 24-32) alone vs AGE + AGE² (precomputed quadratic) compared via likelihood-ratio test and Wald test on AGE².
- **Models:** primary logistic regression (statsmodels `Logit`, `cov_type='HC1'`); LPM as `sm.OLS` with HC1 SE; auxiliary multinomial regression (`MNLogit`) on the three-way savings state.
- **Controls:** GENDER (MALE dummy), log(1+INCOME), BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC. INCOME log-transformed to absorb right skew (skewed 0–1057, max ≫ median 37.4). SAMESAVE handled only via the multinomial auxiliary, never as a binary-DISSAVED regressor.
- **Diagnostics / robustness:** (i) LR test linear vs quadratic age; (ii) LPM Wald test on AGE² (p=0.059, consistent); (iii) bootstrap CI (B=200) on the AGE partial-dependence and AME; (iv) sensitivity to mean-imputation (rows where INCOME or BMI equals its column mean); (v) subgroup decomposition using a multinomial logit; (vi) AME averaging across the empirical covariate distribution for both logit and multinomial coefficients.
- **Headline numbers:** AGE coef (full N) = −0.0467 (p < 0.001); OR 0.954/yr (95% CI 0.937–0.972); AME = −0.84 pp/yr; LPM coef = −0.0084 (p < 0.001); LR-quadratic p = 0.045; non-imputed-only coef = +0.0001 (p = 0.99); multinomial AME (save-more, same, save-less) = (+2.47, −1.59, −0.88) pp/yr full sample / (+0.10, −0.05, −0.04) pp/yr non-imputed.

Limitations (explicit): narrow age window (24–32), single 1989 cross-section, no survey weights, no marital / employment / education / parity controls, INCOME scale undocumented (no dollar interpretation), and the dominant negative age effect in the full sample is largely an artefact of mean-imputed INCOME/BMI rows.
